safety.en: Roadside running, exposed edges and 30 to 35°C heat made this a demanding outing. I badly underestimated the combination.

scenery.en: Vineyards, olive trees, flowing roads and big views across the Chianti hills. Plenty of wow moments.

surface.en: Enjoyable asphalt and flowing bends, although road quality does not create extra space beside traffic.

access.en: Around 900 m of climbing over 33.5 km, steep descents and limited roadside room. I would not recommend this loop to beginners.

experience.en: I loved the landscape and roads, but the heat made this my hardest ordinary training run. A cooler, shorter outing would be a better plan.

en.title: Tuscany: a hot hilly run
en.excerpt: 33.5 km, around 900 m of climbing and relentless summer heat. Beautiful Chianti roads, a tough lesson in pacing the hills, and kindness at Castello di Albola on another run.
en.body:
Beautiful roads, huge views and some absolutely brutal hills. This was a long run during marathon training, and it became the hardest ordinary training run I have done so far. The climbs were one part of it. The other was the sun beating down in roughly 30 to 35°C heat.

This was indeed Tuscany: the loop links the Chianti hills around Albola and the Radda in Chianti area with the roads towards Badia a Coltibuono, Cavriglia and Neri. [Cavriglia sits at the foot of the Chianti mountains, on the Valdarno side](https://www.visittuscany.com/en/towns-and-villages/cavriglia/). So this is a story about this particular hilly corner of Tuscany, rather than every kind of running the region offers.

I love roads that flow up and down through the landscape. There were bends, vineyards, olive trees and views that kept making me think, wow. I was enjoying all of that while also wondering how much more climbing my legs had left in them.

## The loop: 33.5 km and about 900 m of climbing

The full loop was 33.5 km, with about 900 m of elevation gain. It is a loop, with two big uphill blocks and more climbing late on. There is very little that I would describe as a long, easy, flat stretch.

The opening climb takes you from roughly 440 m to just over 720 m in the first 4.5 km, on the high roads above Albola. The longer descent then runs down past the Albola area towards La Villa, just outside Radda in Chianti. Around 5 to 10 km, the profile drops from roughly 700 m to about 380 m. That is easier on the breathing, but the downhill still asks plenty of the legs.

From the La Villa side, the road rises eastwards towards the Badia a Coltibuono area. This is the other big uphill block: roughly 10 to 17.5 km, climbing back to around 690 m. There are small breaks in the gradient, but the overall direction is very clear.

The roads on the Cavriglia side bring a long descent, especially around 19 to 26 km. Farther on, the return through Neri is rolling, with another noticeable rise during the last few kilometres. By then, with the heat on top of everything else, even a smaller hill felt much bigger.

![Elevation profile of the 33.5 km Chianti loop, with Albola, La Villa, the Coltibuono area, Cavriglia and Neri marked approximately](/assets/uploads/tuscany-chianti/elevation-profile.svg "33.5 km for the full loop, with approximately 900 m of climbing. Place labels are approximate; small elevation fluctuations are filtered from the gain estimate.")

## Great asphalt, limited room for mistakes

The asphalt and the flowing bends were exactly the sort of road running I enjoy. But I was running beside traffic, and some stretches were close to a steep drop. Admiring the view and watching the road both needed my attention.

I would not choose this particular loop as a beginner’s introduction to running on holiday. The sustained climbs, descents and roadside exposure already make it demanding, before adding the heat. On this outing I did not even see cyclists. That is just what I saw that day, but it says something about how solitary the run felt.

![A 10 per cent gradient road sign and a vineyard entrance marked Cantalici](/assets/uploads/tuscany-chianti/chianti-gradient-and-cantalici.jpg "Hills and vineyard views from my time in Chianti. The right-hand photo shows Cantalici.")

The winery in the right-hand photo is [Cantalici](https://www.cantalici.it/en/our-lands/). I went there on a separate visit, away from this loop. It was a beautiful place, and I would recommend visiting it in its own right, running shoes or no running shoes.

Wild boar were another thing on my mind in this area. I was certainly not interested in testing my pace against one on these hills.

## When the heat became too much

Towards the end of the long run, I was so overheated that I went into a livestock barn beside the road and put my head into the animals’ drinking trough to cool down. I cannot even remember whether they were pigs or something else. That was how exhausted and hot I had become. It is part of the honest story of this run, rather than a cooling strategy I would recommend copying.

There was another episode on a different day. Near the end of a run, I accidentally went about 6 km in the wrong direction. By the time I realised, the heat and hills had left me too worn out to run all the way back.

I found [Castello di Albola](https://albola.it/), the wine estate in Radda in Chianti shown in my photo. The people there were lovely: they gave me something to drink and helped me cool down. Then I called a friend to collect me by car. Not the return journey I had planned, but I was very grateful for their kindness.

![The entrance to Castello di Albola in Radda in Chianti, with a cypress-lined drive](/assets/uploads/tuscany-chianti/castello-di-albola.jpg "Castello di Albola, where I found some very welcome help on a separate run.")

## Beautiful, difficult, and worth treating with respect

I really liked running here. The scenery and winding roads were special enough that the toughest training run I can remember still left me with good memories. But enjoying the place does not mean that the way I ran it, in that heat, was a good plan.

If I came back for this loop, I would want a cooler time of day, a much clearer plan for drinks and an easier way to shorten the run. The landscape gets full marks from me. The combination of steep hills, road edges and heat asks for rather more care.
en.imageAlt: A collage of winding asphalt roads, cypress trees and vineyard views in the Chianti hills of Tuscany
